summary: As the canonical RFC format changes from plain text to XML, several publication formats will be rendered from it. This informational document defines the HTML format that will be rendered for an RFC or Internet-Draft.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains what the web page version of an RFC should look like and how it is structured.

what html version do rfcs use
subtitle: The rules for the self-contained, strict-subset HTML version of every RFC and Internet-Draft.

tldr.problem: The canonical RFC format is moving from plain ASCII text to XML, and the RFC Editor needs a defined HTML rendering of that XML.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a strict subset of HTML5 for RFCs: UTF-8, valid HTML, one embedded CSS, stable anchors on paragraphs and sections, and a mapping from each XML element to HTML.
tldr.outcome: It is a non-canonical publication format whose details are expected to change as the tools mature, and it has been updated since by RFC 9920.

today: RFC 7992 is an Informational document from the IAB and has been updated by RFC 9920. The RFC itself warns that its details were expected to change.

sections.title: Why an HTML Format
sections.content:
As RFC 7990 describes, the RFC Series is changing, and one change is that the RFC Editor publishes a non-canonical HTML version of RFCs. This document defines a strict subset of HTML appropriate for RFC Series documents.

Layout is set by a cascading style sheet that is included in the HTML file and described in RFC 7993. The RFC warns that the details, especially vocabularies, are expected to change as the new tools are built. Other implementers must not expect those changes to stay backwards compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: RFCs are getting a web page version. This RFC says exactly which web page building blocks are allowed, and warns that the rules may change.

sections.title: Design Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements build on RFC 6949. Among them:

  • The HTML must render correctly on a list of browser versions kept up to date by the RFC Editor, and display adequately in at least one text-based browser.
  • It uses a subset of HTML that is widely implemented, likely to stay so, and unlikely to cause security issues.
  • The document is self-contained, with no external files for images, CSS or JavaScript, so it can move over email, FTP or rsync without breaking.
  • JavaScript is limited. It may not overwrite or change any text, and any text it adds must be clearly marked as additional.
  • Readers can override the default CSS locally.
  • Every heading and paragraph gets a stable, linkable anchor, and sections should be easy to split into separate files, which will help creating EPUB documents.
  • The abstract must be marked so search engines extract it as a summary.

Accessibility requirements say key information must stay available to people with impaired vision, people who have difficulty distinguishing colors, and people on small screens such as cell phones.
sections.plainLanguage: The web page has to work everywhere: in old text-only browsers, on phones, for people who cannot see well, and even when emailed around. It must carry all its own parts so nothing goes missing.

sections.title: HTML Version and Syntax Rules
sections.content:
The starting HTML version is HTML5, and the RFC Editor will periodically decide which version tools reference. The program that turns XML into HTML follows these rules:

  • Output is UTF-8 and valid HTML.
  • Attribute values use double quotes unless HTML forbids quoting.
  • Lines end only with a line feed (U+000A). Tab, form feed and carriage return characters may not appear.
  • Comments in the XML are not copied to the HTML.
  • The output is pretty-printed with consistent rules.

None of these rules change how the page looks. They are meant to make text comparison tools such as diff easier to write.
sections.plainLanguage: These are tidy-writing rules, like always using the same kind of quotation marks and line endings, so computers can compare two versions easily.

sections.title: Anchors, Pilcrows and the Front Matter
sections.content:
An XML element with an anchor attribute becomes an HTML element whose id has the same value. Each paragraph, artwork or sourcecode segment outside a figure or table also gets a pilcrow (U+00B6) in an a element of class pilcrow, linking to that element. It is normally invisible until the element is moused over.

The front matter starts with <!DOCTYPE html> and a root html element with lang set to en. The head carries a meta charset of utf-8, the title, and meta elements for author, description, generator and keywords. It also holds a link to the XML source, a link to the license, and the embedded style element.

For local tweaks the head also links a style sheet named rfc-local.css in the same directory, which overrides the embedded one. A hidden table of class ears helps printing, and document information goes in a dl with id identifiers. A table of contents follows in a nav element when the XML asks for it.
sections.plainLanguage: Every paragraph gets a tiny link mark that shows up when you point at it, so you can share a link to exactly that paragraph. The top of the page holds the label information, like a title page.

sections.title: Body, Back Matter and Elements
sections.content:
The main body is produced by the per-element rules in Section 9. The back matter holds an optional index, built only if the XML asks for it and has iref elements, the authors' addresses, and further document information.

Section 9 covers each XML element in turn with an HTML example. For instance, text artwork is rendered inside a pre element in a div with classes such as artwork and art-text, and angle brackets and ampersands must be escaped. SVG artwork is included inline. Other artwork would use a data: URI in an img element, but such images are not yet allowed in RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: After the main text come the index and the authors' addresses. A long list then explains, one piece at a time, which web page tag each part of an RFC turns into.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is brief. RFCs are sometimes exchanged outside the normal web sandboxing, for example by using rsync to a mirror site and then loading the file locally. Because of that, more care must be taken with the HTML than is ordinary on the web. This ties back to the limits on JavaScript and external files.
sections.plainLanguage: Because these pages get copied around and opened straight from a computer, they have to be extra careful about what they are allowed to do.
